Hi all,

During Community over Code in Glasgow, we discussed authentication in
Iceberg REST and concluded that we should downscope the OAuth2
AuthManager v2 initiative.

The general feedback was that v2 contains too much new surface at
once, especially grant types. Support for complex legacy behavior
(e.g. vended tokens) also unnecessarily clutters the implementation,
and some people suggested dropping that as well.

I therefore propose to reboot the initiative, with a much smaller scope in mind:

- One single grant: client_credentials.
- Two client authentication methods: client_secret_basic and client_secret_post.
- Simplified token renewal (by re-running the grant before expiry).
- Reduced support for legacy v1 (migrate common properties, but leave
the rest out).

The above scope fits in one PR, so here it is:

https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18756

I truly hope we can get this released in Iceberg 1.13, so that users
can finally benefit from a standards-complaint OAuth2 manager in
Iceberg REST.

Let me know your thoughts.

Thanks,
Alex

body:
Hi all,

Following up on the "should V4 manifests be Parquet-only?" thread [1], I'd
like to continue the discussion here about supporting various data file
formats in V4.

*Should we stop writing new ORC and Avro data files in V4?* Note that this
would only affect new writes; existing ORC and Avro files in upgraded
tables would still be readable.

I've been thinking about this in two dimensions, with more details at the
end of the email.

Feature gaps:
ORC and Avro don't fully support some of the features we've been adding,
and our own format TCK already lists what each one is missing [2]. For
example, neither supports variant shredding, and the current draft of the
vector type spec doesn't support ORC. This also came up last year in #13060
[3] which proposed validating file format compatibility for V3 tables.

Upstream activity:
Both projects are maintained, but there's limited activity on the formats
themselves. The last format changes we needed actually came from folks from
the Iceberg community: Gang added geo types to ORC, and Fokko added
nanosecond timestamps and fixed-size UUIDs to Avro. Otherwise, the features
we need aren't being worked on, so I don't expect these gaps to close on
their own.

At a high level, the questions for the community are:

   1. Should we stop writing new ORC and Avro data files in V4?
   2. What does it mean for Iceberg to support ORC and Avro in V4? If we
   keep them, are we okay with users not being able to use some V4 features
   with them, as is already the case in V3?
   3. If we stop writing them, what bar should a format meet to be writable
   again in a future version?
   4. Are there any users of ORC or Avro data files today? What are your
   thoughts about using these in V4 versus Parquet?

I'd love to hear your thoughts!

Best,
Kevin Liu

[1] https://lists.apache.org/thread/fym02576n5sqy298fjxl0xmsv9z5rb7y
[2]
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/6951360ec8a01644d3c24824ab635e06a82f8a7c/data/src/test/java/org/apache/iceberg/data/ReadFormatModelTests.java#L190-L212
[3] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13060
[4] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/18386
[5] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18387
[6] https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#appendix-a-format-specific-requirements
[7]
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/6951360ec8a01644d3c24824ab635e06a82f8a7c/orc/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/orc/ORC.java#L114-L117
[8] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18416/files
[9]
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/6951360ec8a01644d3c24824ab635e06a82f8a7c/core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/avro/AvroMetrics.java#L35
[10] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17119
[11] https://lists.apache.org/list?[email removed]:lte=1y:
[12] https://github.com/apache/orc-format/commits/main/specification
[13] https://lists.apache.org/list?[email removed]:lte=1y:
[14] https://lists.apache.org/thread/ds0gm18b8cghotv4xtsmgo2ybghht60m
[15]
https://github.com/apache/avro/commits/main/doc/content/en/docs/++version++/Specification/_index.md
[16] https://lists.apache.org/list?[email removed]:lte=1y:
[17] https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/commits/master
[18] https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/pull/624

*More details*

Feature gaps that block a V3 feature or a proposed V4 feature:

   - ORC
      - Default values (V3): our integration can't read them [2]
      - Geometry and geography types (V3): our integration can't read or
      write them [2]
      - Variant type (V3): writes currently fail in Spark [4], and the
      pending fix only turns the crash into a clear error [5]
      - Variant shredding (V3): not supported, per the spec [6], so we
      don't produce variant bounds for ORC files either
      - Table encryption (V3): our integration rejects the encrypted files
      that table encryption produces, so ORC can't be used in
encrypted tables [7]
      - Vector type (proposed for V4): marked as not supported in the
      current draft of the vector type spec [8]
   - Avro
      - Variant shredding (V3): not supported, per the spec [6], so we
      don't produce variant bounds for Avro files either
      - Geo bounds (V3): Avro can store geo types, but the Avro data files
      we write have no column metrics (there's been a TODO for this since 2021
      [9]), so they don't carry the bounding boxes used for pruning
   - #13060 noted in May 2025 that "Parquet is currently the only file
   format that supports all the required capabilities for v3 compatibility"
   [3]. It was approved but never merged, and Avro has since closed some of
   those gaps, such as geo types [10].

Upstream activity in the last 12 months:

   - ORC
      - Dev list: no technical discussions, only release votes and admin
      threads [11]
      - Format spec: unchanged since Gang added geo types in April 2025 [12]
   - Avro
      - Dev list: the technical threads were about the language SDKs, not
      the format [13]. The only two questions about the format itself got no
      replies, including one about standardizing a vector type that came out of
      our vector work [14]
      - Format spec: unchanged since December 2024. The last
      Iceberg-related changes were Fokko's nanosecond timestamps (Dec 2023) and
      fixed-size UUIDs (Jan 2024) [15]
   - Parquet
      - Dev list: roughly 100 technical threads [16]
      - Format spec: added a FILE type, ALP encoding (in preview), and NaN
      counts [17], and a vector type is being discussed [18]

body:
Hey folks!

I've been working on a proposal aimed at enabling an ecosystem of Puffin
blob types, with opinionated (but hopefully lightweight) metadata about
configuration, scope, and how future blobs interact with deletion and
compaction.

For context, separate from any Iceberg specifics, I've been daydreaming
about an idea of "progressive indexing" for a few years: after a file is
written, perhaps weeks or months later, we may discover that read workloads
could be much faster and/or more efficient if we'd made different indexing
choices before. Unfortunately, it's hard to predict whether any such change
might impact ingest workloads, and rewriting data, while commonplace on
small files during early compaction eras, is a non-starter for files that
are large and old, so some read-heavy workloads are stuck with scanning
huge volumes of data that often has high-selectivity features lurking in
dusty corners.

While building out an early, as yet unpublished version of the progressive
indexing idea, I realized that while I was initially focused on the
_timing_ of index builds (still important!) I hadn't spent enough time on
the _diversity_ of available indexes, and how to rein in the predictable
chaos if my earlier goals were achieved and such choices became broadly
available.

So, in recent days, this proposal has evolved to focus on what I now
consider a prerequisite for the timing and diversity visions, which is: how
do we construct and operate an ecosystem that would support the desired
diversity, within guardrails that make the chaos less likely and more
contained, in which query accuracy can be safeguarded as long as
implementers play by the rules?

I have looked at the parallel v4 proposal for secondary indexes, and I
believe my proposal is complementary, even though there are significant
overlaps in scope. In particular mine focuses mainly (but not exclusively)
on filters, or "negative" indices, in which an out-of-date index merely
costs efficiency (i.e. a file/chunk that does not contain rows that satisfy
the predicate is scanned), whereas the `scalar` index described in the v4
proposal is a "positive" index, in which much more care is required to
prevent mutations from corrupting indexes, which would cause query
correctness problems. Section 12 of my proposal is a detailed comparison.

This email is already long enough, so rather than go into further detail,
I'll ask you to have a look at
https://github.com/acruise/iceberg-indexing-ecosystem/blob/main/docs/proposals/puffin-blob-types-and-compaction.md
which is admittedly far too long, just like this email!

Hi all,

The spec is ambiguous about Parquet data files that carry field IDs for
some fields but not all, and no two of the four implementations I checked
resolve such a file the same way. I'd like to agree on one reading and
write it into the spec.

Column Projection [1] says a reader should "use schema.name-mapping.default
metadata to map field id to columns without field id", which reads as per
column. The paragraph that follows says the mappings "provide fallback
field ids to be used when a data file does not contain field id
information", which reads as per file. For a file with no IDs at all, both
readings agree. They diverge when only some fields carry an ID.

What the readers do today, on their main branches:

- Java (ReadConf, ParquetSchemaUtil.HasIds): if any field in the file has
an ID, the file is resolved by ID only and the name mapping is not
consulted.
- PyIceberg (pyarrow_to_schema, _HasIds): IDs are used only if every field,
including list elements and map keys and values, has one; otherwise the
whole file is resolved through the name mapping.
- iceberg-rust (arrow/reader/pipeline.rs): the first top-level column
decides; if it has an ID, the file is resolved by ID only.
- iceberg-go (table/internal/parquet_files.go, pruneParquetSchema.fieldID):
Parquet column pruning resolves per field; an embedded ID wins, and the
mapping fills in the fields without one.

This happens in practice. Delta tables with column mapping, written without
IcebergCompatV2, store IDs for top-level columns but none for map keys and
values or list elements. When such a table gets Iceberg metadata [2],
PyIceberg reads the map columns through the name mapping, while the Java
reader resolves by ID only and does not find the map's key and value. The
same table gives different results depending on the reader.

I propose the per-field reading, which matches the Column Projection rule:
a field with an embedded ID is resolved by that ID, and a field without one
falls back to the name mapping. It never overrides an ID a writer recorded,
it changes nothing for files with full IDs or with none, and it makes the
partial case readable.

If there is agreement, I can open a spec PR that clarifies the paragraph,
and contribute a fixture to iceberg-verification [3]: a file with IDs on
its top-level fields only, as a companion to the base name-mapping table
that issue covers.

Is there a reason for the per-file behaviour that I'm missing, for example
a correctness concern with mixing ID and name resolution within one file?

[1]
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/%23column-projection&source=gmail&ust=1793746430284000&sa=E
[2]
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://github.com/apache/incubator-xtable/issues/911&source=gmail&ust=1793746430284000&sa=E
[3]
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://github.com/apache/iceberg-verification/issues/14&source=gmail&ust=1793746430284000&sa=E

Thanks,
Sylwester

Hi all,

I'm a contributor to Apache Polaris. We have a question about the REST
catalog's metrics endpoint (POST
/v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/metrics, reportMetrics)
that we'd like to settle with the Iceberg community before changing server
behavior.

*Background*

Polaris can persist metrics reports sent to this endpoint. Today, if the
database write fails, the endpoint returns a 500. A pending Polaris PR [1]
would log the failure, increment a drop counter, and return 204 instead.
The motivation is that a degraded metrics store shouldn't show up as a
catalog failure. The discussion on the Polaris dev list [2] has split on
this.

*What the spec says*
The spec defines the operation as "Send a metrics report to this endpoint
to be processed by the backend". It documents 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 419,
503 and 5XX. It doesn't say whether reporting is best-effort or whether a
catalog must signal a failure to process a report. It also doesn't say what
a client should do on a 5xx.

*What clients do*

As far as I know, the Java client's REST metrics reporter catches and logs
errors from this endpoint and does not retry. I haven't checked the other
implementations (PyIceberg, iceberg-rust, iceberg-go), so please correct me.

*The two readings*

*1. Best-effort telemetry.* The client sends the report and moves on. A
catalog may drop a report it can't persist, as long as it surfaces that to
operators. A 5xx tells the client nothing it can act on.

*2. A normal REST write.* If the catalog can't process the report, it says
so with a 5xx, and clients may retry. This matters for anyone using the
reports for auditing or billing, though it only helps if clients actually
retry.

*Questions*

1. Is reportMetrics intended to be best-effort? Is a catalog allowed to
accept a report and discard it, or fail to process it, without signaling
failure?
2. If a catalog can't process a report, what should it return? Is 5xx the
expected answer, or is 204 acceptable?
3. Should clients be expected to retry a failed report? If so, the spec
should say that. If not, it should say reporting is not guaranteed delivery.
4. Should the spec state any of this in the endpoint description, so
implementations behave consistently?

We'd like to follow whatever the community decides rather than invent
Polaris-specific behavior. I'm happy to send a spec PR with clarifying
wording once there's a direction.

Thanks,
Anand

[1] https://github.com/apache/polaris/pull/5395
[2] https://lists.apache.org/thread/0r7fpq153d2ny0tbt162051dh0jv3wjb

The metrics endpoint and metrics reporting is intended to be best-effort
and the RESTMetricsReporter implementation also ensures it does not bubble
up any errors.
I don't think we want reads/writes to fail just because the server couldn't
store information about the scan/commit.

endpoint because those are all potential errors. It is up to the catalog
implementation to decide whether to throw a 500 or just log an error. The
catalog can also decide to discard metrics reports and return 204.

overall duration of a scan/commit and we don't want to negatively affect
the read/write path.

I don't think we need to explicitly define the behavior as best effort in
the spec.  The endpoint has defined behavior and return codes.  It being
separate from a commit inherently makes it a separate operation
disconnected from the commit itself.  The idea of "best effort" is probably
misleading here.  The critical operation is the commit.  Metrics are
separate and reporting is not required for the commit.

reasonable for the server to return a code that doesn't represent what
actually happened within the request.  Returning a success code when
there's a failure is clearly wrong and an implementation issue.  However,
whether a client retries or ignores the failure response from the metrics
endpoint is a client-side implementation issue.

I played with Steve's suggestion, and I think it's the right
direction. Here are the main ideas:

Hi Dan and Russell,

A proposal to close the API question: replace catalogName(String) with
hadoopConf(Configuration), with Dan's FileIO lookup as the default. I agree
with Russell that catalogName does not say what it controls.

   - hadoopConf(Configuration) on DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction is the
   Hadoop configuration the listing uses, replacing the session configuration
   when set. RemoveOrphanFilesProcedure passes the session configuration plus
   the spark.sql.catalog.<name>.hadoop.* overrides of the catalog it was
   invoked on, which is what SparkUtil.hadoopConfCatalogOverrides already
   builds for SparkCatalog. The action keeps wrapping it in
   SerializableConfiguration and no longer knows about Spark catalog names.
   - Default, per Dan's suggestion: when hadoopConf is not set and table.io()
   is HadoopConfigurable, use the configuration it holds; otherwise the
   session configuration as today. For tables loaded through SparkCatalog that
   is the session configuration plus the catalog's hadoop.* overrides, so
   HadoopFileIO and ResolvingFileIO users get the fix without calling
   anything. This reads the configuration the FileIO was built with, so there
   is no name-based catalog lookup and no catalog loading side effect,
   which is what the PR review rejected. It is a change from what I said on
   the PR, that nothing changes without opting in; I think it is the right
   default since it is the configuration the table already reads and writes
   with. Say so if you would rather keep it opt-in.

It is still one public method, on the Spark action only, not on the
DeleteOrphanFiles interface. The procedure is in a different package, so it
has to be public. Going through the generic option(...) map was discussed
in the PR review and set aside as the same thing stringly typed, and the
action already takes an arbitrary location, so a typed setter for the
configuration it lists with adds no new capability.

The default alone does not cover #17860: as in my last reply, S3FileIO,
GCSFileIO and ADLSFileIO are not HadoopConfigurable, so the listing would
still use the session configuration and fail with AccessDenied. The
spark.sql.catalog.<name>.hadoop.* overrides are the only per-catalog place
a user can configure the Hadoop FileSystem the listing uses, so the
procedure passes them. As agreed in the review, the fix stays limited to
those explicit overrides; hadoopConfCatalogOverrides keeps its contract and
the action does no credential derivation. prefix_listing does authenticate
through table.io(), but it lists serially on the driver into a single
partition (#16932, #17387), so it is not a drop-in for large tables; making
it parallel is a separate change.

Does this shape work for you? If so, or if there are no objections by the
end of next week (November 15th), I will push it to #17862 this week,
retarget the PR to the 4.2 module, ask yangshangqing95 to re-review since
his approval was on the catalogName shape, and follow with the 4.1, 4.0 and
3.5 backports. The action tests move from catalogName to hadoopConf, plus
one for the default path on a HadoopConfigurable FileIO, and
spark-procedures.md gets the default rule. If you would rather see
something else, a pointer before I rework it would help.

Thanks,
Sebastian

Hi Russell,

Point 2 of my earlier reply does work for HadoopFileIO and ResolvingFileIO,
agreed. So the shape would be: when table.io() is HadoopConfigurable the
listing uses its configuration; otherwise, it uses the session
configuration as today.

What it does not fix is the case in #17860 itself. For Glue the default
FileIO is S3FileIO, and S3FileIO, GCSFileIO and ADLSFileIO are not
HadoopConfigurable. A stock Glue catalog with a cross-account role
therefore still lists with the cluster identity after this change and still
gets AccessDenied. The user has three ways out: io-impl set to
ResolvingFileIO, io-impl set to HadoopFileIO, or prefix_listing. The first
keeps S3FileIO underneath and only borrows the Hadoop configuration for the
listing:

spark.sql.catalog.tenant.io-impl org.apache.iceberg.io.ResolvingFileIO
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.client.factory
org.apache.iceberg.aws.AssumeRoleAwsClientFactory
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.client.assume-role.arn
arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/lakehouse-access
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.hadoop.fs.s3a.aws.credentials.provider
org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.auth.AssumedRoleCredentialProvider
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.hadoop.fs.s3a.assumed.role.arn
arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/lakehouse-access
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.hadoop.fs.s3a.assumed.role.credentials.provider
com.amazonaws.auth.WebIdentityTokenCredentialsProvider

It works, but it asks the user to change their FileIO to fix a maintenance
procedure, and to declare the role twice because the listing authenticates
through s3a while everything else goes through the SDK.

The second option, HadoopFileIO with the same hadoop.* keys, puts listing
and table I/O on one identity path, but every read, write and delete then
goes through s3a instead of S3FileIO: deletes drop from DeleteObjects
batches of up to 1000 keys to one call per file, and the s3.* catalog
properties stop applying. A fallback, not the IO the AWS docs recommend.

The third option, prefix_listing, is the right path for a non-Hadoop IO,
but today it lists serially on the driver into a single partition (#16932,
#17387), and on Spark Connect that also runs into
spark.rpc.message.maxSize, which a client session cannot raise. So for
S3FileIO users the correct path does not scale and the scalable path has
the wrong credentials.

Two possible follow-ups, and I would like a steer on which fits:

1. Make ResolvingFileIO the default FileIO for the Glue catalog, as it
already is for REST. For s3:// locations it delegates to S3FileIO with the
same properties, so the data path is unchanged, but table.io() becomes
HadoopConfigurable and the stock Glue case is covered by the shape above.
The catch is that ResolvingFileIO needs Hadoop on the classpath, which the
AWS module does not require today, so that is a question for the AWS
maintainers.

2. A parallel prefix listing on the executors, so that prefix_listing gives
S3FileIO users the same scalability as the Hadoop walk, with the table's
own credentials and no s3a configuration at all.

If the HadoopConfigurable shape is what you want for #17862, I will rework
it against the 4.2 module and follow with the 4.1, 4.0 and 3.5 backports.

Thanks,
Sebastian

Thanks, Russell, for your time on this, I'll try my best to explain.

If you select GlueCatalog as IcebergCatalog and no io-impl, by default you
get S3FileIO as io-impl (
https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/1.5.1/aws/#s3-fileio).
Now, if you have Spark running in AWS Account A with a base IAM Role A (say
IRSA or Pod Identity), and the lakehouse (Glue + S3) in AWS Account B, and
you need to chain assume IAM role B from A to access data in account B
(think of a multitenant setting), everything works
except remove_orphan_files as it will still use IAM Role A (and fail with
access denied - this is the bug we want to solve).

Right now, the DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction constructor
<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/5329317ad465d81dd940768d6c6b903044e58935/spark/v4.2/spark/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/spark/actions/DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction.java#L136>
takes
a SparkSession object and a Table object, and initializes hadoopConf as new
SerializableConfiguration(spark.sessionState().newHadoopConf()).
newHadoopConf()
only sees spark.hadoop.* properties, dropping the catalog. This is why it
ends up using IAM role A.

In my PR I added a public `catalogName` method
to DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction and changed the hadoopConf property to
non-final so that one could figure out the correct hadoopConf tied to the
catalog. Daniel suggested extracting the hadoopConf from Table.io()
instead, thus avoiding changes to the class's public interface. However,
this would only work if the FileIO implementation (io-impl) is
either HadoopFileIO or ResolvingFileIO. As I said, by default it is
S3FileIO, which has no hadoopConf.

So a user needs to know that, when configuring a Glue catalog with
cross-account access, they also need to change the io-impl to ResolvingFileIO
just so that remove_orphan_files works correctly.

Hi Alex,

I'm +1 generally speaking. Also, I think it's a good idea to hide Jackson
behind Iceberg types, it's a good cleanup (not directly related to Jackson
3).

Reading your points, I have a few comments:
1. About the ordering and "mixing" Jackson 2 and 3, I would do the shims
first (your items 3 and 4) while they are still backed by Jackson 2. We
could deprecate the Jackson typed API in 1.13 (I'm thinking especially
HTTPRequest.mapper() and HTTPClient.Builder.withObjectMapper()). The switch
to Jackson 3 then becomes an internal change, and we ship both Jackson 2
and 3 for a short time. Bundling both is not really a technical problem:
they use different packages, and the Spark/Flink runtime jars already
relocate com.fasterxml, so we just need a tools.jackson relocation. It just
makes the jar bigger and more "exposed" (CVE, etc).
2. Rather than writing new tests, I would parameterize the existing parser
tests (TestSchemaParser, REST request/response parser tests, ...) to run
against both Jackson 2 and Jackson 3 during the transition, They already
cover the JSON contracts. Also, comparing the serialized output of Jackson
2 & 3 would also catch the default feature changes in Jackson 3.
3. I would be very very careful on your point 4, about the REST layer. REST
catalog servers register the serializers on the ObjectMapper. Polaris, for
instance, does that with Quarkus mapper, and Quarkus is moving to Jackson
3. These servers can't avoid Jackson completely: they need a Jackson module
to plug into their mapper. Also, RESTSerializers exposes about 20 public
nested serializer/deserializer classes that extend Jackson types, not only
registerAll(). So I don't think shims alone are enough here. The "separate
artifacts" idea from your first email (and Steve legacy module) fits this
part well. Core would stay binding agnostic, and small adapter modules
(something like iceberg-rest-jackson2 and iceberg-rest-jackson3) would each
expose a Jackson module. Servers pick the one they need.
4. I agree with the splitting. I would suggest:
- introduce the shims and migrate the parsers package by package (several
PRs, I would be happy to help there)
- the REST layer
- dual binding tests and Jackson 3 switch
- removal of the deprecated Jackson 2

Happy to help there!

Regards
JB

Hi Roman,

I think it's a good idea to clarify this.

I checked the Java side. DateTimeUtil.nanosToMicros has used Math.floorDiv
since timestamp_ns / timestamptz_ns were first added, and Bucket hashes
that result. I also recomputed the example: hashing -1 µs gives bucket[100]
= 12, and hashing 0 µs gives 76. So floor division is what the reference
impl has always done. Since Java, Go and Rust (now) all agree, I see this
as a clarification of existing behavior, not a format change.

I have a couple of suggestions on the PR (I will cast there too):
- Put the rounding rule straight into note 3 so all the conversion
requirements stay in one place, something like "Nanosecond timestamps must
be converted to microsecond precision before hashing, by dividing by 1,000
and rouding toward negative infinity (floor division) to ensure timestamps
have the same hash value".
- Add a pre epoch test value to the timestamp_ns and timestamptz_ns rows,
for example 1969-12-31T23:59:59.999999999 ￫ 1651860712 (that's
hashLong(-1)). Truncate toward zero would give 1669671676 instead, so the
table itself would catch any implementation that gets this wrong.

I will review the PR.

Thanks!

body:
Hi guys,

Thanks for bumping this thread (I just saw that thanks to Dan :)).

I agree with Dan: authorization should drive the request shape, and it's
easier to settle it now.

A few thoughts:
- If the server needs context to authorize a FILE reference, it has to be
per element, as a batch can span several data files and columns. I would
keep the top level properties as it is and add an optional context on
RemoteSignBatchElement. Mixing client provided context with server provided
static properties in the same map would be confusing imho.
- If servers rely on this context to autorize, all clients (Java, Python,
Rust, ...) have to send the same thing, so I think it should be defined in
the spec (for instance data file location and field ID) and not as opaque
keys in a map. I would also use the field ID rather than the column name:
names change on rename and are ambiguous for nested fields.
- The context is a claim from the client. The server can check that the
caller has access to the column (and maybe that the data file is part of
the table), but it can't verify that the URI is actually referenced in that
file without reading it. So for shared storage, the server still needs its
own control (for instance allowed locations for a FILE column), and the
spec should be clear that the context helps the decision but is not a proof
by itself. On the cost side, elements sharing the same (data file, field
ID) can be authorized once, so the cost scales with the number of distinct
pairs, not with the number of rows.

Per element authorization also answers the partial results question from
the PR review: with shared storage, some elements of a batch can be signed
while others are denied, so the completed/failed split makes sense.

I’m also not sure to standardize AI functions in the Iceberg expression
spec. The spec deliberately defines a small, engine-neutral expression
model, with common predicates and a limited set of portable functions
closely tied to Iceberg’s needs (ie, data organization and skipping). It

adoption easier.

require agreement on semantics such as model identity, versioning,
inference configuration, and determinism. I’d prefer to use the existing
function/UDF mechanisms unless there is a clear Iceberg-specific need for a
standardized contract.

Hi JB and Dan,

Thanks for the reviews. I agree we should be clear on how authorization for the FILE type works for a REST catalog server, and that the interface supports those semantics.

The initial batch api proposal assumes, like the existing access delegation endpoints, that the server authorizes the request's principal against the table.

Regarding Dan's point on including more granular auth context into the request: since an external FILE reference originates from a column in a data file, I can see why we'd want that context to be in the authorization input. I think JB made some great observations on this topic:

1. The context would be an optional, spec-defined input (data file location and field ID), kept separate from the server-provided `properties`.
2. Use field-id over column names
3. It is a claim from the client. It informs the server's decision but is not proof, so for shared storage the server still needs its own control and verification.

Because the context is optional, adding it later does not change the behavior of clients and servers that don't use it, and a server that needs it can refuse requests without it. So I think we can treat it as an enhancement rather than block the batch API on it.

I think where the context lives is still an open question. JB makes a good case for defining it at the element level in `RemoteSignBatchElement`, since a batch can span several data files and FILE columns. But keeping it at `RemoteSignBatchRequest` would keep elements smaller, at the cost of clients grouping by data file and field.
Either way we could add it as an optional context, and if we do support it, I think it's also worth considering the feature across other access delegation modes (like vended credentials).

That's my thought on this specific requirement. But that being said, I'm happy to keep this thread open while the FILE implementation settles, so we capture authorization semantics we haven't thought of yet.

Here is a summary of yesterday's index sync. Thanks to everyone who joined.

1. Derived columns
Péter asked whether derived columns (for example, storing Hilbert values in
the index) should be index-only or part of the table spec, and whether in
V4 or V5.

   columns will move forward in parallel, as a separate effort building on the
   existing derived columns proposal.

   derived columns reach consensus, the index spec picks them up through the
   shared schema.

2. Index REST spec (#16963)
Agreed:

   - Nest index routes under the table:
   /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/indexes[/{index}], with
   index names unique per table, plus an optional endpoint to list indexes in
   a namespace.
   - Indexes are sub-resources of their table. Renaming a table moves its
   indexes with it, and dropping a table drops its indexes. How the catalog
   removes them is up to the implementation.
   - Multi-table indexes are out of scope.

   access. The read restrictions section should state that read restrictions
   must be applied whether a client reads the table, the index, or both, so an
   index never exposes data the caller could not otherwise see.

   round trips when the table is loaded for reading. But most loads (for
   example, catalog federation and UIs) don't need full index metadata, and
   producing it on every load adds cost. Options discussed: return indexes by
   default, return them only when the client asks (possibly with only index
   names by default), or distinguish read-path loads from metadata-only loads.
   Clients that don't understand indexes can ignore the extra field either way.

body:
Hi guys

I checked the Java side, and it matches what you both described:
- ParqueSchemaUtil.hasIds() returns true if any field at any depth has an
ID, so a file with only top level IDs never uses the name mapping.
- It does the same per file check with ORCSchemaUtil.hasIds().
- Avro already works per field. AvroSchemaUtil.getFieldId() uses the ID in
the file when there is one and falls back to the mapping when there is not.

For the Java change, removing the hasIds() branch won't be enough. When a
path matches, the Parquet and ORC ApplyNameMapping visitors set the ID from
the mapping and overwrite any ID already in the file. They will need to
keep an ID that's already there and only fill in the missing ones.
Otherwise, "never overrides an ID a writer recorded" is not true.

I think the spec should cover a mapped ID that collides with an embedded ID
on another column of the same file. I believe that can happen with an
outdated or hand written mapping, and then two columns resolve to the same
field ID. This case only exists with the per field reading, because today
readers use either IDs or the mapping for the whole file. Maybe we could
make embedded ID wins and the conflicting mapped ID is ignored, so that
column is treated as having no ID. Failing the read would also be fine.
Either way, we should be explicit in the spec.

Something like that in the spec: "These mappings provide fallback field ids
for fields in a data file that do not have a field id. A field id stored in
the data file always takes precedence over the name mapping."

Manu proposed a PR for the spec, I think it makes sense.

Regards
JB

required for any
implementation to be correct. The divergence comes from readers treating
"does this file use field IDs?"
as an all-or-nothing switch for the whole file.

Iceberg writers don't produce files with only some field IDs (so the Delta
behavior is unexpected),
but if a reader encounters one, resolving each field independently, with
the file's ID taking precedence over the mapping, is unambiguous and safe.

The other cases raised are different: they describe a file where two
columns resolve to
the same ID, which is undefined behavior. It is like adding a name mapping
for a file with
columns A, B, C and mapping all three to ID 1 ({A -> 1, B -> 1, C -> 1}).
That is a user error,
not something the spec should require you to check for.

In general we shouldn't tell implementations how to fail when they
encounter an illegal file.

body:
After digging into the history, the per-file reading is the original
intent, and I'm less supportive of widening it.

I ('m the problem, it's me) added the name mapping text in 2021 (#3542
<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/3542>, #3556
<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/3556>). The intent was always the
whole file:

*"These mappings provide fallback field ids to be used when a data file
does not contain field id information."*
The use case was files from Hive and other plain Parquet writers that don't
write field IDs at all, which is why the rest of that section talks about
imported data files.

The per-column wording ("map field id to columns without field id") came in
with #10835 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/10835> in 2024, when we
clarified identity partition values
and initial-default. Name mapping was split into its own resolution step
there, but we weren't trying to change its scope, and partial files weren't
discussed.

Iceberg writers are required to store field IDs for every field, so a file
with only some IDs isn't a valid Iceberg data file. From this thread,
the only source of these files is Delta tables using column mapping without
IcebergCompatV2. Delta only assigns IDs to struct fields,
and IcebergCompatV2 exists specifically to add the missing IDs for list
elements and map keys and values.

So the proposal would change behavior we've had since 2021, based on a
sentence added unintentionally in 2024, to support files from a
Delta configuration that isn't meant to be Iceberg compatible. It also adds
a new requirement for every
implementation (per-field resolution, never overwriting embedded IDs, and
defining what happens on collisions).

I'd rather fix the 2024 sentence to match the original meaning: the name
mapping applies to data files
that don't contain field IDs. If we want name mappings to apply to files
that have only some IDs, I think that's a new feature,
and we should start from the use cases. So far the only one I've seen is
Delta. This may be valid, but let's restart this as a discussion
of a new feature then instead of a spec clarification.

Hi everyone,

Ahead of the iceberg-go v0.8.0 release candidate, I propose a short list of
issues and PRs to resolve before the RC is cut. Each of them is an absolute
P0: it can return wrong results, bring back deleted rows, or leave a table
that can no longer be read. Each issue has a reproduction, and the first
five were re-checked against iceberg-go main (7cf76392).

Issues to fix before the RC:

1. #2604: A merge-on-read Delete on a table upgraded from v2 to v3 brings
back rows deleted before the upgrade. The new deletion vector does not
include the older position deletes, and readers skip position deletes once
a DV exists.
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/issues/2604

2. #2605: After an identity partition source column is promoted (int to
long, float to double), a v2 merge-on-read Delete commits, and from then on
Go scans that read that partition fail. 0.7.0 rejected the same delete
instead.
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/issues/2605

3. #2606: After a partition spec change, a v2 merge-on-read Delete of a row
in a file written under the old spec writes its position delete file under
the new spec. Go scans that read the file then fail, and iceberg-java 1.12
rejects the table as corrupted.
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/issues/2606

4. #2609: UpdateSchema does not require last-column-id to be unchanged, so
a stale AddColumn can reuse the field ID of a column another writer
dropped, and the new column then reads that column's old values. It becomes
reachable with the new default of 4 commit retries (#2462). If the
fix can't land in time, keeping the previous default of 0 retries would
avoid it.
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/issues/2609

5. #2610: After a float identity partition column is promoted to double,
equality deletes written after the promotion are silently ignored for files
written before it (v2 and v3).
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/issues/2610

6. #2596: Partial Parquet row-group statistics on imported files can make
scans skip matching rows and make copy-on-write deletes remove rows outside
the filter. Fix: #2597.
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/issues/2596
7. #2485: Identity partition columns that are not stored in the data files
(for example, Hive-style imports) are read as null, and copy-on-write
rewrites can move rows to the null partition. Fix: #2487.
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/issues/2485

8. #2537: Committing the same RowDelta builder twice duplicates rows. #2602
may cover this, but that is not verified yet.
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/issues/2537

PRs to merge before the RC:

1. #2597: omit incomplete Parquet statistics (fixes #2596)
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/pull/2597

2. #2487: fill identity partition columns missing from data files (fixes
#2485)
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/pull/2487

3. #2602: reject duplicate data paths in RowDelta, including after a retry
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/pull/2602

4. #2599: reject orphan cleanup and purge when snapshot history was loaded
with "snapshot-loading-mode=refs"
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/pull/2599

5. #2601: reject snapshot expiration with refs-only snapshot history
https://github.com/apache/iceberg-go/pull/2601

#2605 and #2610 share a root cause: partition values from manifests written
before a type promotion keep the old type and are compared without
widening. Reading older manifests with the current partition type should
fix both.

#2600 widens values for deletion vectors and fixes the int-to-long case of
#2605, but not the float case or #2610, so a focused fix for these two
seems better than holding the release on #2600.

I am open to discussing the prioritization or deprioritization of any of
the above, and would love to hear your thoughts. I'm also happy to work on
fixes and help with reviews.

Thanks,
Badal Prasad Singh

Hi everyone,

Following the discussion on the dev list [1
<https://lists.apache.org/thread/zpl1pk6v7k49s30gmm3kr986bc9y7jyv>] and
the review on GitHub, I'd like to call a vote to adopt the Materialized
View specification in PR #11041 [2
<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/11041>]. The PR adds a
"Materialized Views" section to the View spec (format/view-spec.md),
along with the storage table metadata it relies on.

Summary of the change:
- A materialized view is an Iceberg view whose version carries a pointer
to a storage table. The storage table is a regular Iceberg table that
holds the precomputed results.
- Readers that do not understand materialized views ignore the pointer
and evaluate the view query directly, so existing view consumers keep
working unchanged.
- Refresh state is recorded in the snapshot summary of the storage
table. It captures the view version that was materialized, the refresh
start timestamp, and the state of the source tables and views at refresh
time (snapshot IDs for tables, version IDs for views).
- Consumers use the refresh state to decide whether the storage table is
fresh. When it is stale, a consumer may fail, refresh, or fall back to
the view query, but must not read from the storage table.

Background:
- The design follows the community's earlier decision to model a
materialized view as a separate Iceberg view and Iceberg table rather
than a new combined catalog object [3
<https://lists.apache.org/thread/qlvtb3wzp8yvx4jbxzpydf7rr3mvjzcq>].
- Proof-of-concept implementations in Spark and Trino validate the spec
[4 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/9830>][5
<https://github.com/trinodb/trino/pull/31027>]. Thanks to Marius Grama
and Walaa Eldin Moustafa for building them, and to everyone who reviewed
the proposal [6 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/10043>] and
the PR over the past two years.

Since this adds new metadata to the spec under format/, it requires a vote.

The vote will be open for at least 72 hours.

[ ] +1 Adopt the Materialized View spec
[ ] +0
[ ] -1 Do not adopt (please provide reasons)

Here's my +1 (non-binding).

Best,
Jan Kaul

body:
Hi all,

I'd like to start a discussion on adding initial snapshot load to Spark streaming reads.

Today a Spark streaming query with a fresh checkpoint can only replay the table's history from the oldest ancestor snapshot. This is slow for long-lived tables, and it cannot work once snapshots have been expired. Currently there is no way to read all data files in the current snapshot before continuing incrementally, which is a common pattern in streaming tables and has been part of the Flink connector since v0.14.0 with StreamingStartingStrategy set to TABLE_SCAN_THEN_INCREMENTAL.

https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18068 adds this feature to Spark streaming through a new `stream-from-snapshot` option:

  - unset (new default): initial snapshot load - read the current snapshot in full, then continue with new snapshots
  - “earliest" (current default): read snapshots starting from the oldest ancestor
  - “latest": only snapshots committed after stream startup
  - "<snapshot-id>": from that snapshot, inclusive

`stream-from-snapshot` and `stream-from-timestamp` would be mutually exclusive.

There is still an open question regarding if this behavior should be the new default. The PR currently makes initial snapshot load the default, which changes behavior for existing queries that start with a new checkpoint. The alternative is to keep today's default and make initial snapshot load opt-in.

Thanks,
Alex

body:
Hi everyone,

I want to start a discussion about what "deterministic" means for functions
in stored expressions, and what the UDF spec should say about it.

Why this matters

Some features compute a value when data is written, and compute it again
later, maybe in a different engine:

   - Check constraints (v4): a UDF used in a check must set `deterministic`
   to true.
   - Stats-only fields in the index spec (
   https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16961): the expression must be
   deterministic. The writer uses the value to sort index entries. The reader
   computes it again to find the right region file.
   - Derived (generated) columns: the value is computed from other columns
   when data is written. Different engines may write rows to the same table,
   so they must compute the same value for the same input.

If two engines get different results for the same input, a check can pass
in one engine and fail in another. An index lookup can also miss rows. For
a primary key lookup, a missed row means a duplicate row is written.

What the UDF spec says today

   - `deterministic` is a boolean on each definition version. The spec
   doesn't say what it means: the same result within one query, within one
   session, or always.
   - "Deterministic" can be a weak requirement or a strong requirement. The
   weak one is a hint for the engine to optimize, for example to cache a
   result. The strong one is "the same input always gives the same output".
   The `deterministic` flag in the UDF spec is meant as the weak one.
   - A UDF can have one SQL body per engine. Nothing says these bodies must
   return the same result. This came up in the UDF spec PR, and the decision
   was to follow the view spec and not add a rule:
   https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14117#discussion_r2771641415.

What other systems do

   - "Deterministic" has two meanings in practice. The SQL standard,
   Oracle, Db2, MySQL, Snowflake (IMMUTABLE), BigQuery (JavaScript UDFs) and
   PostgreSQL (IMMUTABLE) mean "always the same result for the same input".
   Spark and Trino use a weaker meaning: both treat current_timestamp() as
   deterministic, because its value is fixed within one query. This is close
   to PostgreSQL's STABLE.
   - Session settings can change results. PostgreSQL says a function that
   depends on the time zone should be STABLE, not IMMUTABLE. Oracle warns that
   changing NLS settings in a session can give wrong results from a
   function-based index. SQL Server requires fixed SET options for indexes on
   computed columns. Db2 doesn't allow functions that depend on special
   registers in generated columns.
   - In almost all systems, the flag is a promise from the person who
   creates the function. The system doesn't check it. If the flag is wrong,
   results can be wrong.
   - For stored data, many systems don't allow UDFs at all, even ones
   marked deterministic: Delta generated columns and CHECK constraints,
   Snowflake virtual columns and materialized views, BigQuery materialized
   views, MySQL generated columns and check constraints, Db2 expression-based
   indexes, and Oracle check constraints. Some systems do allow UDFs:
   PostgreSQL in indexes and stored generated columns, if the UDF is marked
   IMMUTABLE; Oracle in function-based indexes and virtual columns, if it is
   marked DETERMINISTIC; and SQL Server in indexed computed columns, if SQL
   Server decides the function is deterministic.
   - The databases above each run one engine, so they don't need multiple
   engines to agree. Delta is also used by many engines. The Delta Lake docs
   say generated column expressions can't use user-defined functions, and the
   Databricks docs say the same for CHECK constraints.

Options
1. Add a new optional flag to the UDF spec for the strong requirement (name
TBD, default false). When it's true, the function returns the same result
for the same input in any engine, session, or environment, and all its SQL
bodies return the same result. Check constraints, stats-only fields, and
derived columns would require this new flag instead of `deterministic`.
This is similar to PostgreSQL and Oracle: UDFs are allowed, and we trust
the person who creates them.
2. Do what Delta does: only allow functions defined in the Iceberg spec,
and no UDFs.

Option 2 is simpler and safer, but it's too limiting. For example, sorting
an index by a Hilbert curve value needs a function that Iceberg doesn't
have, and we want to keep the list of Iceberg functions small.

Open questions

1. What should the new flag be called? `immutable` matches PostgreSQL and
Snowflake, but people may confuse it with immutable view and UDF versions.
2. What about functions that are not UDFs? Stored expressions can also call
SQL standard functions and engine built-in functions, and the new flag
doesn't cover them. For example, lower() can depend on locale. Should we
only allow Iceberg functions and UDFs with the new flag? Engines can wrap
their own functions in UDFs.
3. Should the new flag also mean `deterministic` is true?

If people agree with adding a new flag in UDF spec, I can open a PR for
this.

Thanks,
Huaxin

Thanks Huaxin for putting this together.

I would like to suggest another option: *add an optional **volatility**
enum* with three values: VOLATILE, STABLE, and IMMUTABLE, with semantics
based on PostgreSQL's volatility categories [1].
We could deprecate the existing *deterministic* flag and define its
relationship with volatility during a transition period.

Pros:

   - Covers both the existing weaker notion of determinism and the stronger
   guarantee needed here.
   - Provides a clear, established distinction without introducing another
   overlapping boolean.
   - Can be used for other cases where STABLE is sufficient.

Cons:

   - Slightly more complex than a boolean.
   - Adding enum values in the future may have forward-compatibility
   implications.

I would prefer this option because it provides a clean distinction between
the different guarantees and is more expressive than adding another boolean
flag.

Thanks,
Peter

[1] PostgreSQL Function Volatility Categories:
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/xfunc-volatility.html

Thanks Huaxin, I think this question is a bit overdue.

There are multiple places where this matters: derived columns, check
constraints and stats-only fields all hit the same question, so answering
it here is important.

I think determinism is a must wherever a value gets computed again later.
But forbidding UDFs closes too much. It just pushes people back to
engine-specific table properties.

+1 to Peter's enum idea, with some more thoughts:

1/ The key rule is "computed again later", not the function itself. Check
validation, virtual columns and stats-only expressions need to be
IMMUTABLE. A value computed once and stored as the source of truth can be
VOLATILE: defaults, materialized derived columns. They are very useful with
AI functions like embed(body, 'my-awesome-model'). They can be
non-deterministic, but they can't be virtual.

2/ IMMUTABLE means no hidden inputs. Session time zone, locale or collation
version must be explicit arguments. That also covers built-ins: wrap them
in a UDF declared IMMUTABLE.

3/ deterministic=true is IMO closer to STABLE, not IMMUTABLE. Readers
should treat unknown values as VOLATILE.

4/ Allowing UDFs shouldn’t mean every engine has to support them. An engine
that can’t evaluate a stored expression ignores it on read (falls back to a
scan) and refuses to write, same as any unsupported feature.

best,
Andrei

body:
+1 (non-binding), with two questions/concerns/comments and my apologies for
the last-minute engagement. I believe both concerns can be addressed by
language changes rather than anything deeper.

1. The summary in the first email says a consumer that finds the view stale
"must not read from the storage table" but I couldn't find that in the PR
at bf43793.
Both PoCs address this concern by comparing the refresh state's
`view-version-id` with the view's current version before applying any other
test (Spark in `isFresh`, Trino ahead of its grace period), but although
the proposed spec language mentions `view-version-id`, I couldn't find
language that requires readers to check the version before relying on the
storage table snapshot.

More fundamentally, the proposed language doesn't say what happens to the
storage table when the query changes:
 * the Trino PoC keeps the same storage table and empties it;
 * the Spark PoC rejects `CREATE OR REPLACE`, with a comment that the spec
leaves this open.

I'm not sure offhand if there's any other way to change the query in a
preexisting MV definition; perhaps some kind of ALTER?

An engine that kept the storage table without emptying it, and used Example
1's staleness window, would answer queries against the view from the old
query's results until the window ran out. Engines are free to use their own
freshness criteria, but maybe the proposed spec language should require the
comparison both PoCs already make.

2. Snapshot summaries aren't inherited, so a compaction or manifest rewrite
of a storage table leaves its current snapshot without `refresh-state`. The
spec doesn't say what a reader should conclude, and each plausible answer
has a cost:

   - *If the reader treats the view as stale*, every compaction throws away
   the last refresh. The next query evaluates the view query in full until
   someone refreshes, and an incremental refresh has nothing to start from, so
   it becomes a full one. A storage table compacted nightly is stale every
   morning.
   - *If the reader looks back for the last snapshot* with `refresh-state`
   (which the new "presence of a snapshot with `refresh-state`" sentence could
   be read as inviting), it can serve wrong results. That happens when
   anything other than a rewrite was committed in between, such as a row-level
   delete for compliance, or a write from an engine that doesn't know the
   table is a storage table.
   - The outcome also *depends on which engine* did the maintenance. The
   Trino PoC carries refresh-state forward in its own OPTIMIZE, so the same
   view stays fresh after a Trino compaction and might go stale after anyone
   else's--I haven't checked whether the Spark PoC follows suit.

*Candidate normative text:*

1. An engine evaluating a materialized view must not use the view's storage
table in place of the view query unless the `view-version-id` of the
`refresh-state` it relies on equals the view's `current-version-id`,
regardless of the engine's freshness criteria.

2. The `refresh-state` an engine evaluating a materialized view relies on
is that of the current snapshot of the storage table, or else of its
nearest ancestor that has one, provided every later snapshot is a `replace`
operation. If a later snapshot has any other operation, or no such ancestor
remains, the engine must treat the storage table as never refreshed. The
sentence on using "the presence of a snapshot with refresh-state" to
distinguish a never-refreshed storage table would cite this rule.

3. (Optional) A writer committing a `replace` snapshot to a table it knows
to be a storage table should copy `refresh-state` from the parent snapshot,
re-reading the parent on each retry.

Thanks, and apologies if I've misunderstood!

Determinism per se is only one kind of effect/coeffect, and it's easy to
get confused about it.

For example, `now()` and `random()` are carefully documented by most
engines to be evaluated at query start time, and the former might not
strike many people as "nondeterministic" per se even though it makes
queries non-repeatable even under an immutable dataset.

`random()` is more intuitively viewed as "nondeterministic" but
`random(seed=4)` is intuitively "deterministic" but, as with `now()`, when
it's called, and how long it's memoized, matter to query correctness.

More trivially, expressions that are pure (i.e. free of effects or
coeffects) can be memoized forever, whereas an expression that only carries
a "reads a field from a record in a table" coeffect can be memoized just as
safely, but for a shorter timespan.

body:
Thanks Huaxin for starting this. I remember bumping into some of these
challenges when discussing check constraints.

+1 to Peter's volatility enum, with Andrei's rule that readers treat
unknown values as VOLATILE.

blocker to the table function work (check constraint, derived column). The
current Iceberg deterministic should be enough.

The spec already asks for more than the flag promises. A check expression
"must be pure. Its result must depend only on the values of the fields it
references in the row" [1]. The next paragraph requires only that a UDF in
the check declares `deterministic` as true, and the UDF spec defines that
flag as "Whether the function is deterministic" [2]. Spark and Trino treat
current_timestamp() as deterministic, so a UDF that calls it can set the
flag and still break the purity rule. I think the check rule should require
IMMUTABLE instead of `deterministic`.

Iceberg's definition of IMMUTABLE needs three parts that PostgreSQL's
doesn't. An Iceberg UDF can have a different body for each engine, and
engines like Spark, Trino, and DataFusion run it in parallel across many
machines.

1. Every representation returns the same result for the same arguments.
Huaxin's option 1 had this clause, and the enum should keep it.
2. The result depends only on the arguments. It must not depend on session
settings (time zone, locale, collation, or ANSI mode), other rows, row
order, how the engine splits up the work, or how many times the function
runs. For example, Spark's ANSI mode is a session setting [3], so the same
Spark body can fail on overflow in one session and return a value in
another. Even rand(42) in Spark gives different values depending on how the
input is split into tasks [4].
3. Behavior is preserved across definition versions. The check rule already
says this [1].

Representations will rarely disagree on purpose. They will disagree because
a function with the same name behaves differently in each engine. For
example, Spark and DataFusion can return different results for the same
regular expression [5]. An author who writes the same regex call in both
bodies can't see the difference by reading them, so the first part of the
definition is a promise that only testing can back.

should for Immutable be reserved for iceberg/engine functions only?

Iceberg can't check that representations agree, so the only alternative to
trusting the creator is to disallow UDFs. Part of the declaration can be
checked, though. A UDF body is SQL [6], so anything that makes it
non-deterministic has to come from a function it calls, like now() or
rand(). An engine can look at the calls in the body for its own dialect.
Could the spec say an engine must treat a UDF as VOLATILE when that body
calls a STABLE or VOLATILE function? Then only agreement across dialects
rests on trust.

I agree, and distributed engines also compute values again inside the
writing job. When a task fails, the engine runs it again, and the rerun
evaluates the expression again. If a random value decides which partition a
row lands in, the rerun can put the row somewhere else. If other tasks
already read the first attempt's output, the row can be written twice or
lost. Spark detects this and reruns everything downstream [7][8], but not
every engine does. So I'd require IMMUTABLE for a derived column used as a
partition source or in a primary key, even when it is materialized.

This also supports Szehon's point that STABLE has a narrow use. A STABLE
value stays the same across a distributed query only because the engine
computes it once up front and sends the result to every task. Spark does
this for the current time [9], and DataFusion does it for STABLE functions
called with constant arguments [10]. That helps the optimizer, but it says
nothing about what a later query computes, and that is what a stored
expression needs.

Thanks,
Matt

body:
*Background*

The v4 vector type, vector(E, D), stores fixed-length numeric arrays such
as embeddings.
 E is the element type and D is the dimension. A list can hold the same
values today, but
it gives no guarantees about them. A vector guarantees that every non-null
value has
exactly D elements, and that every element is non-null and finite. Writers
enforce these
rules, so readers and engines can rely on them.

The proposed element types are int, long, float, and double. These are
existing Iceberg
primitives so the change is very straightforward. However, we've had
requests for new
types currently not represented in Iceberg, specifically float16 and int8.
We've had a lot of
discussion about the "how" we could add such types but not enough
discussion of "why" and "why now."

*My main focus now is finishing V4. If we can't reach consensus after this
much discussion, I think the only real option is to push this to V5.*

I think there are basically 3 different answers to the "Why" for the new
types

  - Physical Storage
      - Gain: Fewer bytes on disk and over the network
      - Needs: An encoding that does not store 16 bits of padding per value
  - Performance
      - Gain: Less memory, faster scans, faster distance computation
      - Needs: The width in the schema, and an engine with native float16
memory and compute
  - Validation
      - Gain: A guarantee that every value fits in the type
      - Needs: The width in the schema, and writers that enforce it

*Physical storage*
The storage question is this: if the data is already float16, how much
space do we lose when we store it as float?

I measured this on five public embedding sets: OpenAI 1536d and 1024d,
Cohere Wikipedia 768d and 1024d,
and GloVe 200d (chart and data
<https://gist.github.com/RussellSpitzer/d571e3bd5db91b964f021cfcf94f2112>;
I got the datasets from Raincloud <https://github.com/spiraldb/raincloud>).
All values were float16 values. I stored each set as float and as FLOAT16.

Storing float16-valued vectors as float32 doubles their size uncompressed
(32 vs 16 bits per value),
but with dictionary encoding and zstd the float32 column comes to about
15.0 bits per value against 14.7–14.8 for FLOAT16, roughly 2% larger.

With dictionary encoding, float loses almost nothing. The float16 data I
tested has only 25,000 to 35,000 distinct values,
so each value becomes a 15-bit dictionary ID. Even in the worst case, there
are only about 64,000 distinct float16 values,
which would need just 16-bit dictionary IDs.

Peter Vary's synthetic benchmark agrees (results
<https://lists.apache.org/thread/p41hstcw9r702zo9k94qzn67foxbbnzk>). His
values were also float16, and dictionary encoding
 gave about 15.1 bits per value for both float and FLOAT16.

Allowing FLOAT16 as storage for vector(float, D) saves about 2% over a
dictionary-encoded float column. So there is really nothing to gain here.
INT8 is stored as Int32 physical type in Parquet, so there is no encoding
difference between Int8 and In32 data.

*Performance*

If the schema declares float16, a compatible engine can theoretically hold
each element in
2 bytes instead of 4, although this too depends on the engine's memory
representation. We can imagine
 engines that use different in-memory representations, or representations
with some kind of internal encoding.

The engine must still know the width/shape before it reads data.
It sizes buffers and chooses compute kernels when it plans the query. So
the width must be available at planning time.

An engine that decodes float16 to float32 gets none of this gain. An engine
that uses an alternative memory
layout may not benefit either. The gain is also specific to chip
architectures that support SIMD on half-width types.
advantage of this now but if someone
has other targets please let me know.

In our discussions, we also heard that some cutting-edge work needs the
vector type presented to the engine
as a byte array (there are many possible non-list like layouts), in order
to use custom distance metric implementations and similar techniques.
This is basically out of scope for our discussion since that's basically
just Binary and not a well defined type in our system.

*Validation*

A float16 element type also restricts the values a vector can hold. Every
element must be exactly
representable as IEEE 754 binary16. That limits magnitude to 65,504 and
precision to about three decimal digits.
 Writers would enforce this, as they enforce the dimension and finite
values today.

A reader can narrow every value to float16 with no loss. A writer that
produces out-of-range values fails at write time,
not at read time. The vector type adds the same kind of guarantee for
length and finite values.

*Our Choices*

Regarding the 'Why,' it definitely seems like both Performance and
Validation are honest concerns. The question of
"Why Now" seems to be on a bit weaker ground. The Performance argument will
rely on future work in downstream engines
and as I noted may not match the performance requirements of other layouts
or other usecases in the future. Validation
though seems to be a honest requirement for the moment.

Secret Human Note: For all the human readers who got this far, I hope you
are having a wonderful day.

*Given this I think we have the following options:*
*  - No float16 or int8 in v4*
      - We currently lack sufficient information on engines which actually
want to take advantage of this data type. We may be putting the cart before
the horse here without relevant demand. Revisit in v5, when more engines
may have native float16 support. If we don't have consensus on any of the
other options we pick this by default.

*  - Float16 as an allowed storage type for Float*
      - Allows for slightly more compact physical storage. Engines that can
take advantage of physical type awareness at read time can benefit. (I
don't know of any such engines so I would recommend we don't choose this.)

body:
Hi all,

Following up on the question of whether shared source is better overall
than per-version copies, from a maintenance and dependency perspective, I
did a draft POC ( #19025 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/19025> (do
not merge)).

What it does:

   - 545 common source files in 4.1 and 4.2 move to spark/common.
   - Every file that differs stays as a full copy in its version directory.
   - There are no shims, which addresses Xin's governance concern.
   - Each Spark minor still compiles its own jars against its own Spark,
   and the 4.1 and 4.2 runtime jars match main's.
   - It also adds 4.3, with the same adaptations as #18749
   <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18749>.

What I observed since 4.2 landed (Sep 4):

   - 23 PRs changed only 4.2 and touched files this layout would share.
   - 13 of them were later backported to 4.1 by hand. With shared source,
   we would have avoided the backports.
   - 5 PRs used 4.2-only Spark APIs. These are the main 4.2 features. With
   shared source, each would have had to fork the shared files it touched
   first, or wait until 4.1 is dropped. This is the dependency cost Russell
   raised in the sync. Shared code can only use APIs that every member version
   has.

The gains with this approach are the fewer needed backports, but the big
cost is waiting for the last incompatible version to be dropped before
adding a new API.

Also, with AI, copying directories and backporting to older versions is
easier than before. I think we should not pursue this. Let me know if you
think otherwise.

Thanks,
Anurag

Thanks Russ, the numbers help a lot.

I’m +1 on leaving float16 / int8 out of v4 (option 1), and using separate
vector element types later (option 3) if we want them in v5.

   -

   I’d push back on option 2. If float16 is just a storage choice for
vector(float,
   D), the actual encoding becomes a per-file writer choice. Every reader
   has to support all allowed encodings and only finds out which one it got
   when it opens the file. For ~2% size win, that feels like a lot of
   complexity.
   -

   I agree validation is the stronger reason to put the width in the type.
   Options 3 and 4 do that; option 2 doesn’t.
   -

   Spark and Delta don’t have a half-precision type today. Adding a real
   float16 type would mean changes across several type systems before we
   have a concrete need for it. Keeping it inside vector is much cheaper, and
   engines that don’t support float16 can still read through the parent
   type.
   -

   I've started drafting a Delta vector RFC, and the intent is to keep its
   physical mapping the same as Iceberg's: one physical element type for each
   E, and a field id only on the outer group. If v4 starts with int / long /
   float / double, the two formats can stay aligned from the start, and both
   can add element types later.

One thing I’d like in the v4 wording: don’t close the set of element types
in vector(E, D). That way adding a float16 / int8 element type later
doesn’t require inventing a new vector type.

Best,
Andrei

body:
Hi Russell,

Thanks for collecting and structuring all this information. And yes, I am
having a wonderful day :D

One small correction on physical storage: with Parquet byte-stream split
encoding, the difference can be somewhat larger in favor of float16. In my
benchmark, float16 was approximately 10% smaller [1]. The result is
dataset- and configuration-dependent, and is still far from the
uncompressed 2x difference, but I would not conclude that the storage gain
is always negligible.

Given the vector type is primarily motivated by fixed-length vectors in
AI/ML workloads, I think we should evaluate the options from that
perspective.
When I look at type support needed for AI workloads, my first reference
point is Lance which supports both float16 and int8 [2]. My other reference
point is the pgvector which also supports half-precision vectors through
halfvec [3]. From the Microsoft side, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed
Instance, SQL database in Microsoft Fabric, and SQL Server 2025 all support
float16 as an explicit base type [4].

We are actively working on adding Iceberg to our stack. The engines in that
stack support float16, and many of our AI vectors currently use float16 or
int8, so I have a slight bias here.

Wearing only my Apache hat:
*  - No float16 or int8 in v4*
      - Engines with native support for narrow vectors would not be able to
use Iceberg as the authoritative representation without additional
conversion or maintaining a separate Iceberg copy. That pushes users toward
data duplication.

*  - Float16 as an allowed storage type for Float*
      - This provides a physical optimization, but the Iceberg schema would
not communicate the narrower representation. Engines would need
non-standard conventions such as catalog labels, machine readable table
properties or field comments. With additional table-level aggregation,
min/max statistics can tell us whether current values fit within the int8
range. For float16, they cannot tell us whether values are exactly
representable.

*  - Separate Vector Element Types*
      - This covers the main AI use cases because these workloads generally
operate on vectors rather than on individual elements. It also leaves room
for additional vector representations later. My only concern is that the
logical element-type model should remain independent of Parquet, even if
the initial implementation uses Parquet annotations. This is my preferred
V4 option.

*  - Full Types for Float16 and Int8*
      - There is a chicken-and-egg problem in waiting for broad engine
support before adding the types to the table format. Nevertheless, I agree
that requiring general-purpose support for both types in V4 may be
premature.

For these reasons, *I prefer adding separate float16 and int8 vector
element types in V4*, while postponing the decision about making them
general-purpose Iceberg primitive types.

Thanks,
Peter

[1] BSS encoding results:
https://lists.apache.org/thread.html/4bwf1khhjnt4t2vgon5qxrvz8bbcg559
[2] Lance data types: https://lance.org/guide/data_types/
[3] pgvector half-precision vectors:
https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#halfvec-type
[4] Half-precision float support in the SQL vector data type:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/data-types/vector-data-type-half-precision-float

Thanks Peter, and thanks for correction on BSS.

I think it's fine to go with option 3 in v4, with separate float16 / int8
vector element types. Putting the width in the schema handles validation
and the AI use cases Peter mentioned, without adding full Iceberg scalar
types.

A few things I think the spec should make clear:

   -

   Fallback to the parent type should be required. A reader without float16
   support reads vector(float16, D) as vector(float, D), and int8 as int.
   Both are lossless.
   -

   Writers shouldn’t silently narrow. If a writer can’t write float16
   directly, it either verifies the values are exactly representable or
   rejects the write. No implicit rounding from float to float16.
   -

   The element types should stay separate from the Parquet mapping.
   FINITE_VECTOR may be the first encoding, but it shouldn’t define the
   type itself.
   -

   If float16 / int8 later become full Iceberg types in v5, they should
   keep the same names and semantics.

If any of this starts holding up v4, I’d rather ship the base vector type
with int / long / float / double and add the smaller element types in v5.

Best,
Andrei

I think there is broad consensus for Iceberg to support multiple formats.
We don't want to get stuck supporting just one and not have the
abstractions needed to add another when there is a good candidate. I
realize there are people suggesting that we add Vortex, but that's not the
decision we have right now.

The current decisions are whether it makes sense to continue support for
ORC and, somewhat separately, whether it makes sense to support Avro. This
is only "somewhat" separate because we don't want to remove both of them at
once. That would leave us with only one format and I don't _think_ that's
what we want to do.

For the choice of whether we continue to support ORC, I think Kevin's
summary is really helpful. When we considered removing ORC in v3, we said
that we would wait and see if contributors closed the gaps. At this point,
I think we can conclude that the gaps are going to remain and we should not
let the gap widen by allowing ORC to be written in v4 tables.

For the choice of whether to continue to support Avro, I support keeping
it. The biggest reason is that we have consensus about having two formats
and Avro is the clear second format at this point. The format support gap
is considerably smaller than ORC, and not all of the v3 gaps make sense.
For instance, variant shredding doesn't make sense for Avro to implement
because it is a row-oriented format.

I think that there's a clear decision here: we should remove ORC for v4 and
revisit Avro support in the next version.

Ryan

Hi everyone,

The File Type spec introduces support for referencing media and binary
blobs (e.g., images, video, audio, PDFs, tensors) in Iceberg v4, but leaves
open how the table stores, tracks, and garbage-collects those bytes when
managed by the table. Currently, inline Parquet bloats random reads and
compaction, one-object-per-blob hits object-store request limits, and
external blobs remain untracked by ExpireSnapshots and DeleteOrphanFiles.

I would like to share a proposal for Managed Multimodal Blob Containers in
Iceberg v4. This approach allows writers to store small blobs inline, pack
medium blobs into shared blob files, and write large blobs to dedicated
packs. By tracking pack references in manifests, features like snapshot
expiry, orphan cleanup, relative paths, and credential vending can work
without scanning data files.

Please take a look at the proposal and share your feedback:

https://s.apache.org/iceberg-managed-blob

I look forward to hearing your thoughts!

Best regards,
Talat Uyarer
