Hi all,

Andrei, thanks for checking Java. I built that shape into a fixture and ran
it through four readers. The fixture holds the input only and waits on this
thread for its expected values [1]

The data file has field IDs on every top-level column and struct field, and
none on the list element, map key or map value. Its ID'd columns have names
the mapping does not list, so they resolve only by ID. Results:

- Java 1.11.0 (generic Parquet reader): the ID'd columns read correctly.
Any projection that includes the list or the map fails with "... is not in
the store", which confirms what Andrei saw.
- iceberg-go main: every projection fails, including one of only ID'd
columns. Its hasIDs check does not look below a field that has an ID, so
the file counts as fully ID'd and schema conversion fails at the list
element. My earlier "per field" description of iceberg-go does not hold for
nested fields.
- PyIceberg 0.12.0: every projection fails. One missing ID makes it resolve
the whole file through the mapping, which does not list the ID'd columns'
names.
- DuckDB 2.0.0 with the iceberg extension: the ID'd columns read correctly,
the list reads with the right length and every element null, and the map
fails because its required key has no ID.

So four readers give four results, and only two of them return the ID'd
columns at all. With the per-file rule agreed, I'd suggest the wording
settle two more things:

1. In a file that has field IDs, a field without one is not present in the
file. A list or map whose element, key or value is not present reads as
null as a whole. That extends Ryan's "that column is null" to nested
fields, without inventing entries or keys.
2. Whether a field that has an ID can be read does not depend on other
fields of the file lacking one, so a projection of ID'd columns returns
their values. With Andrei's two points (an ID at any nesting level counts,
and the check runs on the file schema), the result no longer depends on the
query.

If the community prefers that such a list or map fails the read instead,
that works for the fixture too. What matters is that the spec picks one.
Andrei, I'm happy to review the spec PR, and I'll write the fixture's
expected values to match whatever it says.

Thanks,
Sylwester

with a certain WHERE filter while allowing it with a different filter
because they affect different files.

within the file format readers.

body:
Thanks everyone for the discussion in today's sync. Since my last message
I've looked at how often engines actually agree, and I'd like to narrow
what I proposed.

Both the current `deterministic` rule and an IMMUTABLE level in the enum
rest on the UDF author promising that every dialect's body returns the same
result. I don't think anyone can keep that promise. Engines disagree on
details the SQL spec leaves open, and nobody knows all of them.

For example, `array_contains(array(1, NULL), 2)` is NULL in Spark and false
in DataFusion and DuckDB. The SQL spec doesn't define `array_contains`,
both answers are defensible, and Spark kept its behavior on purpose [1][2].
Under Iceberg's null-safe comparisons [3], a check like
`array_contains(tags, 'pii') = false` rejects that row in Spark and accepts
it in DataFusion. An author who writes that call in both bodies has no
reason to suspect a difference. `ln(0)` is NULL in Spark and -Infinity in
DataFusion, and their `ln` results differ in the last bit on about 2% of
inputs [4][5][6]. Regex engines differ too [7]. Engines also sort floats
differently around NaN and -0.0, and I filed #19040 [8] for the spec side
of that.

This matches what we've seen on Comet. We've spent over two years making
Rust match Spark for a fixed set of functions, and we still keep a list of
known differences [7]. That's with a reference engine to test against and
fall back to. A UDF author has neither.

Here's what I'd propose now:

1. Stats-only fields and index ordering keys use only functions defined in
the Iceberg spec, each with exact semantics and test vectors, the way
`bucket` works today [13]. A Hilbert curve would become one of these
functions.
2. UDFs stay allowed for values that are computed once and stored, like
write defaults.
3. I still like Peter's volatility enum for UDFs, as long as unknown values
read as VOLATILE and the old `deterministic` flag never maps to IMMUTABLE.

That's close to Huaxin's option 2 for index keys and stats-only fields. It
means a longer list of Iceberg functions. But each one gets specified once,
instead of every pair of engines finding their differences through wrong
results.

Check constraints are the hard part, because the point is to let planners
trust them. The v4 rule already allows UDFs that declare `deterministic`
[9], and each engine runs the body for its own dialect. So a Spark writer
and a Trino writer can both mark a check as valid while running different
code [10]. SQL bodies make this hard to spot, because the differences hide
in built-ins like `array_contains`. Even one dialect isn't stable. Spark 4
turned ANSI mode on by default [11], so the same Spark body can fail on one
version and pass on another. And an engine with no body for its dialect
can't write to the table while the check is enforced [12].

If planners trust check statuses, every engine has to evaluate the check
the same way the writer did. That's the same requirement as index keys. So
I think we have to choose: allow only exactly-specified functions in checks
that planners trust, or say in the spec that planning on a UDF check can
return wrong results when bodies disagree. Today's rule does the second
without saying so. Which do people want?

Thanks,
Matt

Hey folks,

Thank you for chiming in to the topic. I've brought this up in various
syncs as well and the sentiment seems to align. Let me try to summarize it.

*Multiple file formats*
Iceberg should continue supporting multiple data file formats, so we should
keep at least two supported formats.

Let's keep the conversation focused on the currently supported file
formats. Adding new file formats is a separate conversation that we can
pursue later.

*ORC*
There seems to be broader consensus to drop ORC write support in V4.

Existing ORC files in tables upgraded from previous versions would remain
readable as is. No rewrite or conversion would be required to upgrade.

If ORC closes its feature gaps in the future, we can re-evaluate adding it
back to the spec. And we'd use the same criteria as for new file formats,
which are still to be defined.

*Avro*
We keep Avro write support in V4, which keeps us at two formats. Whether to
deprecate Avro is a separate conversation; for now, we're focusing on ORC.

*Next steps*
Please flag anything I've missed or mischaracterized. If there are no
objections, I'll start a vote next week to drop ORC write support in V4.

Best,
Kevin Liu

implementation defaulting to v3. I'll defer to others for the other
implementations.

I think the bar for changing the default format version is two things.
First is table stakes, the implementation changing its default should
reliably support reading and writing the core features of that version,
which I think the Java implementation sufficiently does. Second, there
should be broad ecosystem support. DVs, variant, and row lineage are now
supported beyond Spark in OSS engines like Flink, Trino, DuckDB, and Doris,
as well as across data and cloud vendors (referencing
https://icebergmatrix.org/).

That said, of course support isn't universal yet. Just to name some
examples, my understanding is that Trino still treats v3 as experimental,
PyIceberg and iceberg-rust can read DVs but can't write them or variant
yet, and nanosecond timestamps are still behind in a lot of places, Java
and Spark included. It doesn't make sense to wait for every implementation,
but I do want to make sure we're looking holistically at how the core, most
desired v3 features are supported across the ecosystem.

A default also gives the community a clear signal of where support efforts
are focused. I personally think we're there with v3.

Thanks,
Amogh

I basically agree with all of Dan's points. Most of what's in the doc is
related to implementations, and I don't see anything that really needs to
be codified in the spec.

Reachability of blobs for cleanup is a concern for maintenance procedures,
not the table spec. The issue is that blobs are referenced from rows rather
than tracked in manifests, so orphan file removal would treat them as
unreferenced. As Dan mentioned, this has already been discussed, and there
are two cases.

For blobs the table writes, a writer can put them under a separate path.
Orphan file removal skips that path by default, and an option can do a
row-level scan there: read the file type columns of live data files,
collect the referenced blob URIs, and only delete blobs that aren't
referenced.

For blobs outside the table location, the table only references them and
doesn't own them, so orphan file cleanup on a specific table shouldn't
delete them.

Neither case necessitates new metadata in the spec.

The points on storage layout of the blobs (inline vs a shared pack vs a
dedicated file) are all writer implementation choices. The file type's
(uri, offset, size) can already represent each of these.

The concerns around random reads of inline blobs are really about how
Parquet lays out large values, so I think they're better addressed in
Parquet itself, and there's already active work there.

Thanks,
Amogh

Agree with Matt here on silent disagreement.

This is the real problem, but i don't think that means that we shall
restrict ourselves into spec-only functions everywhere. Stats-only fields
are meant as optimization, so it's fine for an engine to just skip them.
What it can't do now is notice the disagreement itself, array_contains here
is a good example.

One option here is to codify this doubt: store stats computed with a
non-spec function along with the name of the implementation that produced
them (engine or versioned shared library). A reader uses them only if it
can truly understand them; otherwise, it ignores them and scans. Spec
functions need no tag, since they are clearly specified. Engines that share
code (like Trino-based ones) still get the pruning, and nobody gets wrong
results. The good example of such behavior is collation bounds, they
already work this way by embedding collator version.

This also leaves room for an engine to move faster than the spec. An engine
(or group of engines that can share code) can define functions on its own
and use each other's stats. Everyon else ignores them and scans which is no
worse than today. When a function proves useful, it can be moved into a
specified function with exact semantics and test vectors. Puffin blob types
work the same way: open names, readers skip what they don't know.

Best,
Andrei

Hi everyone,

Let me pull out my list again:
1. `Default Values` - Not impacted
2. `Constraints` - Critical, possibility of data corruption during write.
Introduce an 'allow-list', aka only iceberg functions. Reason: Iceberg
needs to ensure that ALL engines produce the SAME result.
3. `Derived Columns` - Critical, possibility of data corruption during
read. Solution identical to `Constraints`
4. `Stats-only` - Not-Critical. Engines can ignore it. Proposal: Store an
identifier that specifies how to reproduce the SAME result.

So basically we 'split' it into 2 classes:
1. Features with expressions that can be either ignored (stats-only) or
that get materialized (default values)
2. Features where reproducibility across engines matters (constraints +
derived)

Regarding `Constraints` and `Derived Columns` as already stated by the
others we need an allow-list of functions with semantics defined by
Iceberg, not just names.
Today that is only `iceberg_functions` (if_else + partition transforms) [1]

One problem that I'm currently seeing is that the expressions spec lets us
write `ColA + ColB < ColC` or `amount * (1 + tax)` via `apply` with
`sql_functions` or a UDF [2].
But it doesn't define what they mean. So we are back to the problem of
rounding, overflow and error handling implemented differently in engines.
Which means we now need to define them as well, raising the question should
we?

Best
Marco

Hi all,

Today a compaction fails to commit if any other transaction added a
position delete to one of the files it rewrote while it was running. The
rewrite is a logical no-op, but RewriteFiles validation can't tell a layout
change from a row change, so minutes or hours of work are discarded and
retried due to conflicts. Under steady write + delete traffic on hot
partitions this happens repeatedly.

I'd like to propose an improvement: the rewrite records how row positions
moved from source to output files, and at commit time translates any
concurrently committed deletion vectors onto the output files instead of
failing.

The idea comes from Commutative Compaction (Douglas & Hellerstein, FORMATS
'26)[1]; Chris and I have been working through the design together. I have
a working Spark implementation with tests and benchmarks and would like to
open a PR once there is agreement on the direction.

More details in the doc:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-8T316SMGNWIGzgid5hn0K6xj7hDDMRquleyuQrj3m8

Would appreciate any feedback on the approach！

Thanks,
Shawn

I think two different things may be conflated here. Matt and Marco are
probably right that some Iceberg expressions may be under-defined (like

interpretation of the content is still engine-specific. A user could just

wouldn't be a UDF spec problem. I think Szehon's comments make sense: if
you are really worried, you lock yourself into an engine-specific UDF, and
engines that don't share that dialect shouldn't write or plan using it. We
cannot annotate our way out of two engines interpreting the same UDF
differently.

index, constraint or generated column, but I don't see any reason for the
spec to forbid it. I don't mind adding a note to the spec that guides on
this, but I don't think it's really a different risk than what should
already be expected for cross-engine SQL in any other circumstance, and I
wouldn't forbid it.

body:
Hi Shawn, Chris,

+1 on the direction. Some background on how Delta handles the same problem,
which may help with the persisted version Grant and Pachu are asking for.
I've been working on row-level concurrency for OSS Delta [1], including
compaction-vs-DML remapping in both directions (fork PRs, not yet upstream)
[2]. That work writes the same tags Databricks does, and I tested it with
Databricks Runtime 16.4 committing to the same table concurrently. The
Databricks behavior below is from my own tests on DBR 16.4 and 18.2.

1. Delta resolves both directions. Databricks documents that on
deletion-vector tables, UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE and OPTIMIZE "cannot conflict
... unless ZORDER BY is used" [3]. A DML that loses to a compaction is
remapped too, not only the compaction. That's Case B: the one an in-memory
map can't cover, and the common shape when a streaming writer deletes while
another engine compacts.
2. The persisted map is small. For compaction, each source file's remove
action carries compactedInto (the output file) and compactionInfo (the row
offset in the output and the source's physical row count). The losing side
replays a DV onto the output by offset, skipping the positions in the
source's own DV, which the same commit removes. That's a few numbers per
source, independent of how many rows are deleted, and resolution took about
150 ms. The Iceberg equivalent would be (source file, source start, row
count, output file, output start), with one entry per output-file boundary.
Explicit gaps are only needed for rows dropped by equality deletes during
the scan.
3. Where it lives: Delta keeps it on the tombstone, not in a side file. The
Iceberg equivalent is the source file's DELETED entry in the compaction
snapshot's manifest. RowDelta already reads that entry when it fails with
"Cannot commit, missing data files"
(MergingSnapshotProducer.validateDataFilesExist). So Case B finds the map
with no extra reads, the map commits atomically with the rewrite, and it
expires with the snapshot. It needs a manifest-entry field, which may fit
the v4 entry design.
4. On Pachu's point about sort and z-order: equality deletes commute with
those rewrites too, while a position map grows toward one run per row under
a sort. Databricks doesn't use a bigger map there; it uses row tracking.
With row tracking on, liquid clustering OPTIMIZE (including real
reclustering and OPTIMIZE FULL) reconciled with concurrent
DELETE/UPDATE/MERGE in both directions. With it off, every such race
aborted. That path is slower: about 2-3 s versus ~150 ms. Iceberg v3
already requires row lineage, and a rewrite must copy each moved row's
_row_id into the new file (spec, Row Lineage), so the same approach needs
no opt-in. A position map for order-preserving rewrites plus a _row_id
lookup for sort/z-order would let DVs cover what equality deletes commute
with today.

I'd be glad to work on the DML side: translating a RowDelta's DVs through
the persisted map during validation. It builds on #17754 and #18603, and
it's on the #18020 roadmap [4].

Thanks,
EJ

[1] https://github.com/delta-io/delta/issues/7360
[2] https://github.com/sezruby/delta/pull/9 (compaction loses),
https://github.com/sezruby/delta/pull/11 (DML loses),
https://github.com/sezruby/delta/pull/12 (persisting the source composition)
[3]
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/isolation/row-level-concurrency
[4] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/18020

Hi Shawn, Chris,

Thanks for writing this up, and thanks Grant, Pachu and EJ for the context
so far. I did a first round of review on the doc. The direction makes sense
to me, and fixing compaction commit failures without a spec change is a
good first step. Below are the main gaps I see at the design level. I'll
leave more detailed comments inline in the doc.

   1.

   The doc doesn't say which public APIs, action options or properties this
   introduces, or whether they live in core or in the engine. Other engines
   and users will build on these, so I think they belong in the doc before the
   PR.
   2.

   The doc refers to Spark's TaskCommit in passing but doesn't state the
   scope of the first version. It would help to say it targets Spark first,
   which parts are engine-agnostic in core, and what another engine such as
   Flink would need to provide.
   3.

   Since this works on deletion vectors, I assume it is v3+ only. Could the
   doc say so explicitly and describe what happens on v2 tables with position
   delete files?
   4.

   The flowchart mentions a "conservative failure or fallback" but doesn't
   define it. When the rewrite can't use the map, does it fail as it does
   today, or skip tracking and commit the old way? Examples are a sort or
   z-order rewrite, a v2 table, too many concurrent deletes, or exhausted
   retries. And should it fail fast when a user explicitly turns the feature
   on?
   5.

   This problem has a long history. #2308
   <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/2308> was the original report,
   #2865 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/2865> added today's
   validation, #3480 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/3480> added
   use-starting-sequence-number, and #5888
   <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/5888> tried rolling back the
   compaction. There is also active DV work touching the same validation code,
   in #17754 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17754>, #18603
   <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18603>, #18224
   <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18224> and EJ's #18020
   <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/18020>. A short section
   comparing these approaches would show why remapping is the right choice and
   how it fits with the in-flight changes.

Persistence of the map requires a spec change and most likely can only come
in V5. One option is to keep this doc focused on the in-memory phase and
add persistence in V5?

As I said, I've been thinking about the same problem, so I'd be glad to
write the design sections and test plan for this doc with you all too if
you'd like.

~ Anurag

Hi all,

Scoping this doc to the in-memory version first makes sense.

On when persistence could land: Anurag suggested V5, but the map may not
need a new format version. The spec increments the version only for
features where "older readers would not read newer table features
correctly" [1]. A reader that ignores the map behaves exactly as today: the
DML fails with "Cannot commit, missing data files". Readers have to handle
a missing map anyway, because writers that don't produce one (older
engines, sort compactions, compactions from before the feature) leave
nothing to translate. Table statistics and partition statistics were added
to v1/v2 the same way, as optional fields. The spec also still lists v4 as
under active development [1]. So the map could be optional in v4. That
would give v4 tables the property Grant and Pachu rely on from equality
deletes, without waiting for V5.

Shawn, for the comparison section Anurag asked for, here's how the
in-flight work relates (#18603 and #18020 are mine):
- #18603 (UPDATE delete-file conflicts) and #17754 (merging concurrent DVs
for pure deletes) are on the DML side and independent of this proposal.
- #18224 adds validateAddedDVs to RewriteFiles. That check already skips
DVs for data files added in the same commit, and the translated DVs here
only reference the rewrite's new output files, so the two don't conflict.
- #18020's compaction section sketches the per-source breadcrumb that Case
B would need.

Thanks,
EJ

Thanks Russell! I posted here specifically because IMO the same analysis
should probably apply to all stored expressions, regardless of their
encoding/representation--at least informally, not necessarily requiring any
specific technical protocol or normative spec language proposal.

UDFs as such can get away with "this string is an engine-specific black
box, you need to be honest about where it can be called, what it might do,
etc." and it's totally defensible to say we're not going to try to parse
it, and thus cannot detect problems. The specific meaning of the
"deterministic" property proposed in the UDF spec is worth digging into,
and my doc spends some time on that.

Other users of stored expressions that use trees rather than deemed-opaque
strings don't have the parsing escape hatch, but every such feature still
needs to set clear requirements about what kinds of expressions they
permit. Determinism per se is important but far from the only kind of
constraint.

meta.subject: DISCUSS] Resolving compaction conflicts with concurrent deletion vectors

title: Re: DISCUSS] Resolving compaction conflicts with concurrent deletion vectors

body:
+1 to not adding a persisted compaction map to the spec until we know it's
actually needed. We can always add an optional field later, so this doesn't
have to block anything. My stance is for this case we should push the
implementations as much as possible before we add spec complexity.

Even before in-memory compaction maps, there are concrete gaps in
maintenance procedures like Spark's RewriteDataFiles that make the problem
referenced above worse than it needs to be. The whole action plans from one
starting snapshot, and every file group validates against it. So each group
is exposed to conflicting deletes from any point since the action started.
On a long running compaction job, groups that start late are very likely to
hit a delete that landed well before they started, which they could have
just read up front. And when a group fails validation we throw its work
away instead of re-planning it against a newer snapshot and retrying.
Spark's position delete rewrite and Flink's rewrite maintenance have the
same pattern, with one baseline for all groups in a run and no retry on
validation failure.

If each group re-planned against the latest snapshot before rewriting,
validated from that same snapshot, and retried on conflict, the conflict
window would shrink to that group's own rewrite time. This keeps the same
isolation we have today, since each group is validated against exactly what
it read.

To be clear about the limits, this doesn't help when a file's DV gets
updated so often that it almost always changes while its group is rewriting
it, like the hot key CDC case. A group can still lose if a delete lands
during its own rewrite, and a retry costs a full rewrite of that group.
That's where the in-memory map may be beneficial. But fixing the baseline
should cut a lot of the conflicts people see today, and it tells us how
much is actually left for a map to solve.

For experiments, I think the useful measurements are commit success rate,
wasted rewrite work, and how much of the table is compacted over time as
the delete rate goes up, comparing today's behavior, re-plan plus retry,
and the in-memory map.

Thanks,
Amogh

body:
Substrait covers the territories of type system and expression
representation; it handles coeffects/effects in a somewhat ad hoc way
though:

* https://substrait.io/expressions/scalar_functions/ describes properties
like determinism, session-dependence, etc. but the built-in function
declarations in the YAML files don't usually include them--it may be that
there just aren't any. Of particular note, there doesn't seem to be a
`random()` function among the standard extension functions!

* aggregate functions are declared explicitly as distinct from scalar
functions, so statefulness can be assumed rather than needing to be declared

*
https://substrait.io/expressions/specialized_record_expressions/#execution-context-variables
describes special handling for timestamps and time zones as "context
variables", not functions (see proto
<https://github.com/substrait-io/substrait/blob/9143f2a89af1efc4daa8180899c57be602d78da0/proto/substrait/algebra.proto#L1821-L1844>),
and the section immediately below provides more generic declarations for
per-plan/per-record evaluation.

Being protobuf-based, Substrait's developer ergonomics when using generated
code are messy--everything is optional-in-theory, a lot of impossible cases
need to be covered to satisfy pattern matchers... A hand-curated library
that wraps the protos is necessary IMO.

Also of note, the relationship between Substrait spec versions, extension
files (where all functions are declared) and extension call sites in query
plans is... probably safe but definitely confusing! Hopefully this is a
correct interpretation:
 - every plan is supposed to carry the version of Substrait it was produced
under, e.g. `0.103.1` (a few months ago)
 - when a consumer processes a plan, it's supposed to interpret function
references found therein as they were declared in the YAML files released
along with the producer's version (
https://github.com/substrait-io/substrait/tree/v0.103.1/extensions -- note
version tag in URL) , which will frequently be different from the version
the consumer was built with. I'm not sure offhand how these are meant to be
resolved; there are routinely breaking changes--fair game in 0.x!

-0xe1a
